steps: Here Maya uploads a fifty row expense spreadsheet, and asks Claude to sum column D.

Claude says about forty-seven thousand three hundred dollars, then forty-six thousand nine hundred and fifty. Maya checks by hand: the real total is forty-four thousand two hundred and eighty-seven dollars. Claude was guessing.
Her manager explains why. A language model predicts text, it does not compute numbers.
So Maya switches on Code Execution, which lets Claude actually run code, and uploads the same expense spreadsheet again.
This time, Claude writes Python code to sum column D, and runs it in a sandbox.
The sandbox returns exactly forty-four thousand two hundred and eighty-seven dollars, across all fifty rows, and Claude shows Maya both the code and its output.
Finally, Maya reads the code and spot-checks a few rows, right file, column D, matching rows, before she relies on it. Exact numbers come from running code.
